concept.name: Consistency
concept.definition: A property of a sequence of estimators: as the sample size grows without bound, the estimates converge in probability to the true parameter value (weak consistency; almost-sure convergence gives strong consistency). The distribution of the estimates concentrates ever more tightly around the truth.
concept.intuition: A consistent estimator is one that is guaranteed to home in on the true value if you feed it enough data - the more you observe, the closer you get, with probability approaching certainty.
concept.mechanics: Formally, T_n is weakly consistent for θ if P(|T_n - θ| > epsilon) -> 0 as n -> infinity for every epsilon > 0. The law of large numbers is the workhorse for proving consistency (e.g., the sample mean is consistent for mu); the continuous mapping theorem carries consistency through continuous transformations.
concept.formula: T_n converges in probability to θ: for all epsilon > 0, P(|T_n - θ| >= epsilon) -> 0 as n -> infinity, where T_n is the estimator based on n observations.
concept.failure_modes: Consistency is an asymptotic guarantee that says nothing about the sample sizes actually available - decades of daily data may still be 'small' for slow-moving parameters. It also collapses under structural change: no amount of data makes an estimator converge to a parameter that itself keeps moving (non-stationarity).
concept.misconceptions: Consistent does not mean unbiased, and vice versa: the n-divisor sample variance is biased yet consistent, while the estimator T_n = x_n (use only the last observation) is unbiased for the mean but not consistent. 'Converges' also does not say how fast.
concept.example: The sample mean of daily returns is consistent for the true mean under stationarity: its variance sigma^2/n shrinks to zero, so with 25 years of data it is tightly concentrated around mu - assuming mu has not drifted over those 25 years.
